claim: Mice were trained to locate an object by active touch with a single whisker (C2).
source: We trained mice to locate an object by active touch with a single whisker (C2) (O'Connor et al., 2010a; O'Connor et al., 2013) (n = 21 mice, 52 sessions; fraction of trials correct, 0.740 ± 0.086; mean ± s.d.; Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the experimental procedure and provides quantitative behavioral performance data (fraction correct) from 21 mice across 52 sessions.

claim: The behavioral task achieved a mean performance of 0.740 ± 0.086 fraction of trials correct.
source: We trained mice to locate an object by active touch with a single whisker (C2) (O'Connor et al., 2010a; O'Connor et al., 2013) (n = 21 mice, 52 sessions; fraction of trials correct, 0.740 ± 0.086; mean ± s.d.; Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of behavioral performance.

claim: Mice whisked in bouts with mean bout duration of 261 ms.
source: Mice whisked in bouts (mean bout duration, 261 ms; peak-to-peak amplitude, 15.7°; frequency, 15.4 Hz) interspersed with periods of rest.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of whisking frequency.

claim: Mice touched the pole multiple times with a mean number of 2.33 touches before reporting perceived object location.
source: Mice touched the pole multiple times (mean number of touches, 2.33) before reporting perceived object location with licking (mean reaction time 367 ± 234 ms; mean ± s.d.) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of touch behavior.

claim: The mean reaction time for reporting object location was 367 ± 234 ms.
source: Mice touched the pole multiple times (mean number of touches, 2.33) before reporting perceived object location with licking (mean reaction time 367 ± 234 ms; mean ± s.d.) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of reaction time.

claim: Recordings targeted excitatory neurons in L4 of the principal barrel corresponding to the spared whisker (31 cells in C2; 10 additional outside C2) and L5 near the principal barrel (11 cells).
source: We targeted recordings to excitatory neurons in L4 of the principal barrel corresponding to the spared whisker (31 cells in C2; 10 additional outside C2) and L5 near the principal barrel (11 cells), guided by intrinsic signal imaging (number of trials per neuron 115 ± 60; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the recording locations and number of cells recorded.

claim: The number of trials per neuron was 115 ± 60.
source: We targeted recordings to excitatory neurons in L4 of the principal barrel corresponding to the spared whisker (31 cells in C2; 10 additional outside C2) and L5 near the principal barrel (11 cells), guided by intrinsic signal imaging (number of trials per neuron 115 ± 60; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of trial numbers.

claim: A typical L4 C2 neuron had a low baseline firing rate of 0.73 spk/s (500 ms before start of sample epoch).
source: The neuron had a low baseline firing (0.73 spk/s; 500 ms before start of sample epoch) that increased substantially during the sample epoch (2.6 fold; to 1.91 spk/s; p = 3.38e-7, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of firing rates for an example neuron.

claim: The firing rate of a typical L4 C2 neuron increased 2.6 fold during the sample epoch to 1.91 spk/s (p = 3.38e-7, Wilcoxon rank sum).
source: The neuron had a low baseline firing (0.73 spk/s; 500 ms before start of sample epoch) that increased substantially during the sample epoch (2.6 fold; to 1.91 spk/s; p = 3.38e-7, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements and statistical test results for firing rate changes.

claim: The Fano factor computed by counting spikes over the entire sample epoch was 7.51.
source: FF computed by counting spikes over the entire sample epoch (stimulus presentation), was huge (FF = 7.51).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative measurement of the Fano factor.

claim: Each touch evoked on the order of one spike (1.51 spikes/first touch; 0.31/later touches) with short latency (onset, 8 ms).
source: Each touch evoked on the order of one spike (1.51 spikes/first touch; 0.31/later touches) with short latency (onset, 8 ms) (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of spike counts and latencies in response to touch.

claim: For L4 neurons in C2, 70.6% ± 20.9% (mean, s.d.) of spikes were coupled to touch in an average of 14.9% of exploration time.
source: Over the L4 C2 population, 70.6% ± 20.9% (mean, s.d.) of spikes were coupled to touch in an average of 14.9% of exploration time.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of spike coupling to touch across the L4 C2 population.

claim: L4 neurons outside of C2 had significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 8.4% ± 13.3% in 3.5% of exploration time (p = 6.53e-6, Wilcoxon rank sum).
source: L4 neurons outside of C2 had significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 8.4% ± 13.3% in 3.5% of exploration time (p = 6.53e-6, Wilcoxon rank sum).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements and statistical test results comparing touch-evoked spikes in different regions.

claim: L5 neurons in C2 showed significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 24.0% ± 18.6% touch spikes in 19.0% of exploration time (p = 2.30e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum).
source: L5 neurons in C2 also showed significantly less touch-evoked spikes, 24.0% ± 18.6% touch spikes in 19.0% of exploration time (p = 2.30e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements and statistical test results for L5 neurons.

claim: For neurons in C2, 75.2 ± 19.0% of spikes were coupled to touch or whisking phase in an average of 22.0% of exploration time.
source: Overall, for neurons in C2 75.2 ± 19.0% of spikes were coupled to touch or whisking phase in an average of 22.0% of exploration time, significantly more than outside of C2 (33.0 ± 30.2 in 16.9% of time; p = 2.88e-4), or in L5 (31.5 ± 16.4 in 26.1% of time; p = 2.96e-5, Wilcoxon rank sum).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements and statistical comparisons of spike coupling to sensory features.

claim: Pooling activity from only fifteen L4 neurons in C2 was sufficient to detect 95% of touches (integration time, 10 ms).
source: Pooling activity from only fifteen L4 neurons (out of approximately 1600 [Lefort et al., 2009]) in C2 was sufficient to detect 95% of touches (integration time, 10 ms) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from decoding analysis and cites the total number of L4 neurons.

claim: A group of 200 neurons in C2, integrating in 10 ms windows after touch, allowed decoding of elapsed time from touch with minimum 0.55 ms uncertainty with 95% confidence at 10 ms post-touch onset using a naïve Bayes decoder.
source: Beyond detection, a group of 200 neurons in C2, integrating in 10 ms windows after touch, also allowed decoding of elapsed time from touch with high precision (minimum 0.55 ms uncertainty with 95% confidence at 10 ms post-touch onset using a naïve Bayes decoder [Duda et al., 2001]) (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from decoding analysis and cites the method used.

claim: A large population of neurons (1000) was required to provide even a rough estimate of whisking phase (24° in C2, 33° outside at d′ = 1 performance, equivalent to 76% correct discrimination).
source: In contrast, a large population of neurons (1000) was required to provide even a rough estimate of whisking phase (24° in C2, 33° outside at d′ = 1 performance, equivalent to 76% correct discrimination) in C2 and the surround columns (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from decoding analysis of whisking phase.

claim: Touch response magnitude was highly modulated by touch order, whisker velocity just before touch, and maximum whisker curvature during touch (mean modulation index: touch order, 0.71 ± 0.25; velocity, 0.71 ± 0.27; max curvature, 0.72 ± 0.23; mean ± std).
source: Touch response magnitude was highly modulated by each of the three variables (mean modulation index: touch order, 0.71 ± 0.25; velocity, 0.71 ± 0.27; max curvature, 0.72 ± 0.23; mean ± std; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of modulation indices for different touch properties.

claim: Responsiveness to pretouch velocity and max curvature covaried strongly (pairwise correlation coefficient 0.80, p = 4.3e-8).
source: Responsiveness to pretouch velocity and max curvature covaried strongly (pairwise correlation coefficient 0.80, p = 4.3e-8), whereas touch order response was somewhat less correlated with velocity and curvature (correlation coefficients 0.70, 0.65, p = 1.0e-5, p = 8.2e-5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of correlation coefficients and statistical significance.

claim: Across the population of neurons within C2, the Fano factor following touch dropped below one, with the FF lying close to the binomial limit for most cells.
source: Across the population of neurons within C2 the FF following touch dropped below one, with the FF lying close to the binomial limit for most cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative observations about Fano factor values and references supporting figures.

claim: Using a narrower touch window of 10 ms reduced the FF to 0.73 ± 0.19.
source: Using a narrower touch window of 10 ms reduced the FF to 0.73 ± 0.19 (Figures 6E, 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of Fano factor under different analysis conditions.

claim: The FF was further reduced to 0.54 ± 0.27 when calculated only across similar touches.
source: The FF was further reduced to 0.54 ± 0.27 when calculated only across similar touches (Figures 6E, 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of Fano factor when controlling for touch similarity.

claim: During object localization, the majority (>70%) of spikes were temporally coupled to touch onset.
source: During object localization, the majority (>70%) of spikes were temporally coupled to touch onset (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative threshold for spike coupling to touch.

claim: The time-scale of temporal modulation (approximately 10 ms) was much shorter than the mean inter-spike interval (approximately 1 s).
source: The time-scale of temporal modulation (approximately 10 ms) was much shorter than the mean inter-spike interval (approximately 1 s).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative comparisons of temporal scales.

claim: Spike count variance after touch, measured using the FF, was close to the binomial limit, the theoretical minimum.
source: Spike count variance after touch (Figure 5), measured using the FF, was close to the binomial limit, the theoretical minimum (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific claim about the relationship between measured variance and theoretical minimum.

claim: L4 responses encode touch with millisecond timescale precision and minimal noise.
source: Based on these criteria we conclude that L4 responses encode touch with millisecond timescale precision and minimal noise.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: L4 contains a precise map, where individual barrels process information from single whiskers.
source: L4 contains a precise map, where individual barrels process information from single whiskers (Simons, 1978).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about barrel cortex organization.

claim: Connectivity within L4 is highly recurrent.
source: Similar to other cortical circuits, connectivity within L4 is highly recurrent (Lefort et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about L4 connectivity.

claim: The only major long-range input into L4 ascends from sensory neurons via the posterior medial thalamus into L4.
source: However, the only major long-range input into L4 ascends from sensory neurons via the posterior medial thalamus into L4 (Lu and Lin, 1993; Bureau et al., 2006; Hooks et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about L4 inputs.

claim: Activity within the barrel cortex is necessary for whisker-based sensation.
source: Activity within the barrel cortex is necessary for whisker-based sensation (Hutson and Masterton, 1986; O'Connor et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies establishing the necessity of barrel cortex for whisker sensation.

claim: Whisker deflections or active touch trigger temporally sharp responses in barrel cortex neurons.
source: Whisker deflections (Simons, 1978; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Jadhav et al., 2009) or active touch (Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; O'Connor et al., 2010b; O'Connor et al., 2013) trigger temporally sharp responses in barrel cortex neurons, which underlie the perception of object location (Diamond et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies establishing the temporal precision of barrel cortex responses.

claim: Spike rates of barrel cortex are modulated by whisker movements on multiple time scales.
source: Spike rates of barrel cortex are also modulated by whisker movements on multiple time scales (Fee et al., 1997; Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing modulation of barrel cortex activity by whisker movements.

claim: Barrel cortex neurons respond with high trial-to-trial variability to passive sensory stimulation.
source: Similar to visual cortical neurons (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Maimon and Assad, 2009), barrel cortex neurons respond with high trial-to-trial variability to passive sensory stimulation (Wang et al., 2010; Adibi et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing high variability in barrel cortex responses to passive stimulation.

claim: Cortical spike trains often appear noisy, with the timing and number of spikes varying across repetitions of stimuli.
source: Cortical spike trains often appear noisy, with the timing and number of spikes varying across repetitions of stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical spike trains that sets up the context for the study.

claim: Spiking variability can arise from internal (behavioral state, unreliable neurons, or chaotic dynamics in neural circuits) and external (uncontrolled behavior or sensory stimuli) sources.
source: Spiking variability can arise from internal (behavioral state, unreliable neurons, or chaotic dynamics in neural circuits) and external (uncontrolled behavior or sensory stimuli) sources.
evidence: The manuscript categorizes potential sources of variability based on established understanding.

claim: Touch was the dominant sensorimotor feature, with >70% spikes occurring in millisecond timescale epochs after touch onset.
source: Touch was the dominant sensorimotor feature, with >70% spikes occurring in millisecond timescale epochs after touch onset.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results.

claim: The variance of touch responses was smaller than expected from Poisson processes, often reaching the theoretical minimum.
source: The variance of touch responses was smaller than expected from Poisson processes, often reaching the theoretical minimum.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by Fano factor analysis in the results.

claim: Layer 4 spike trains reflect the millisecond-timescale structure of tactile input with little noise.
source: Layer 4 spike trains thus reflect the millisecond-timescale structure of tactile input with little noise.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Variability in spike trains constrains how neural computations can be implemented.
source: Variability in spike trains constrains how neural computations can be implemented (London et al., 2010; Renart and Machens, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established theoretical understanding about the implications of spike train variability.

claim: Measured cortical spike trains are often irregular in time, and spike counts vary over repeated presentations of identical sensory stimuli.
source: Measured cortical spike trains are often irregular in time, and spike counts vary over repeated presentations of identical sensory stimuli (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Maimon and Assad, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites established observations about cortical spike train variability.

claim: Noisy spike trains are difficult to reconcile with the integrative properties of single neurons and the high reliability of cortical neurons and synapses.
source: Noisy spike trains are difficult to reconcile with the integrative properties of single neurons (Softky and Koch, 1993) and the high reliability of cortical neurons (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995) and synapses (Stevens and Zador, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies highlighting the paradox between observed variability and known neuronal properties.

claim: This discrepancy has motivated models of cortical circuits that inherently produce noisy spike trains even with reliable neurons, by virtue of chaotic dynamics.
source: This discrepancy has motivated models of cortical circuits that inherently produce noisy spike trains even with reliable neurons, by virtue of chaotic dynamics (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical models developed to explain spike train variability.

claim: Irregular spike trains suggest that spike rates, but not spike timing, are used by the brain for computation.
source: Irregular spike trains suggest that spike rates, but not spike timing, are used by the brain for computation (Mazurek and Shadlen, 2002; London et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical perspectives on neural coding based on spike train variability.

claim: Variability in cortical spike trains is not noise but reflects fluctuating hidden states with possible behavioral significance and uncontrolled experimental factors.
source: Another view contends that variability in cortical spike trains is not noise but reflects fluctuating hidden states with possible behavioral significance and uncontrolled experimental factors (Gur et al., 1997; Kara et al., 2000; DeWeese et al., 2003; VanRullen et al., 2005; Amarasingham et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites an alternative perspective on spike train variability.

claim: Minimizing fixational eye movements in alert monkeys reduces spike count variability in the visual cortex.
source: For example, minimizing fixational eye movements in alert monkeys reduces spike count variability in the visual cortex (Gur et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific example of how controlling behavior reduces variability.

claim: In the sensory periphery, spikes are often coupled to stimulus features with high temporal precision.
source: In the sensory periphery, spikes are often coupled to stimulus features with high temporal precision.
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about peripheral sensory encoding.

claim: Temporal precision allows timing-based neural codes to be faster and more efficient than rate-based codes.
source: This precision allows timing-based neural codes to be faster (Johansson and Birznieks, 2004) and more efficient (Gollisch and Meister, 2008) than rate-based codes.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the advantages of timing-based codes.

claim: Multiple factors can shape neural spike trains, only a subset of which are controlled or measured in typical experiments.
source: Multiple factors can shape neural spike trains, only a subset of which are controlled or measured in typical experiments.
evidence: This is a general statement about experimental limitations in studying spike trains.

claim: Uncontrolled factors will add to measured variability.
source: Uncontrolled factors will add to measured variability (Masquelier, 2013; Renart and Machens, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical understanding about sources of variability.

claim: L4 thus receives little uncontrolled input.
source: L4 thus receives little uncontrolled input.

claim: During natural behavior animals move their sensors to acquire information about the world.
source: During natural behavior animals move their sensors to acquire information about the world (Deschenes et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites established understanding of active sensing behavior.

claim: Measurement of spiking statistics in the barrel cortex is most meaningful during active sensation, when mice shape sensory input by moving their whiskers to solve a tactile task.
source: Measurement of spiking statistics in the barrel cortex is thus most meaningful during active sensation, when mice shape sensory input by moving their whiskers to solve a tactile task.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the appropriate experimental context for studying barrel cortex.

claim: This picture of low noise, rapidly modulated responses differs from the conclusions based on recordings from the cortex of behaving non-human primates.
source: This picture of low noise, rapidly modulated responses differs from the conclusions based on recordings from the cortex of behaving non-human primates (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Maimon and Assad, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript contrasts its findings with previous studies in primates.

claim: Even in cases with time-varying stimuli and corresponding cortical responses with rapid modulation, spike counts vary greatly across trials, resulting in large FFs.
source: Even in cases with time-varying stimuli and corresponding cortical responses with rapid modulation, spike counts vary greatly across trials, resulting in large FFs (Bair and Koch, 1996; Buracas et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous findings of high variability in cortical responses.

claim: In the task, mice control sensory input by palpating the object with their whiskers, and it is likely that mice tune their movements to achieve high signal-to-noise ratio encoding of tactile information.
source: In contrast to passive presentation of stimuli (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Maimon and Assad, 2009), in our task mice control sensory input by palpating the object with their whiskers. It is likely that mice tune their movements to achieve high signal-to-noise ratio encoding of tactile information.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for the low variability observed, based on active control of sensory input.

claim: Loose-seal cell-attached recordings permit accurate sampling of the spike trains produced by the L4 neuron population.
source: Second, by employing loose-seal cell-attached recordings we targeted neurons independent of activity, permitting accurate sampling of the spike trains produced by the L4 neuron population (DeWeese et al., 2003; O'Connor et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites the advantages of the recording method used.

claim: Standard extracellular recordings can have problems detecting neurons with low spike rate and high synchrony.
source: These recording methods could be critical because standard extracellular recordings can have problems detecting neurons with low spike rate and high synchrony (Lewicki, 1998; DeWeese et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites known limitations of alternative recording methods.

claim: During highly synchronous events, such as the population volley after touch, the probability is high that simultaneously recorded units in an extracellular electrode will be missed or misassigned.
source: During highly synchronous events, such as the population volley after touch, the probability is high that simultaneously recorded units in an extracellular electrode will be missed or misassigned (Cotton et al., 2013).

source: Third, compared to measurements from other cortical layers and regions, L4 spike trains in barrel cortex are more easily interpreted because extrinsic input arises mainly from the sensory periphery, rather than other cortical layers or higher cortical areas that might provide input with unobserved dynamics (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explains why L4 is particularly suitable for studying spike train precision.

claim: High temporal resolution tracking of sensory input and whisker movements is necessary to uncover possible influences of behavior on individual spikes.
source: Fourth, we track sensory input and whisker movements with temporal resolutions that are high compared to the inter-spike intervals of L4 cells. This is necessary to uncover possible influences of behavior on individual spikes.

claim: L4 spikes appear irregular when aligned to the sample epoch (coefficient of variation >> 1).
source: Indeed, L4 spikes appear irregular when aligned to the sample epoch (coefficient of variation >> 1, Figure 1C,D; Figure 6E,F).

source: Only after aligning spikes to the fine-scale structure of the sensory input does the meaning of individual spikes become clear (Berry et al., 1997; Baudot et al., 2013).

source: In contrast to L4, only a small fraction of spikes in L5 neurons in the barrel cortex can be interpreted in terms of somatosensory behavior (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific observation about L5 neurons based on the data.

claim: L5 neurons receive multiple types of input with unobserved dynamics representing hidden states.
source: This is likely because these neurons receive multiple types of input with unobserved dynamics representing hidden states (Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites known properties of L5 neurons to explain the observed differences.

claim: The irregularity of the L5 spike trains, as well as spike trains in other cell types and brain areas, may reveal themselves as deterministic fine-scale structure once the multitude of their inputs can be simultaneously monitored.
source: The irregularity of the L5 spike trains, as well as spike trains in other cell types and brain areas, may reveal themselves as deterministic fine-scale structure once the multitude of their inputs can be simultaneously monitored (Gomez et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about future possibilities for understanding spike train structure in other neurons.

source: The irregularity of cortical spike trains has often been interpreted as an irreducible feature of cortical discharges, or noise (Renart and Machens, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a common interpretation of spike train irregularity.

claim: This in turn has led to the view that only spike rates averaged across neuronal populations, but not precisely timed spikes, can be used to perform computations in cortical circuits.
source: This in turn has led to the view that only spike rates averaged across neuronal populations, but not precisely timed spikes, can be used to perform computations in cortical circuits (Mazurek and Shadlen, 2002; London et al., 2010).

source: However, because a large number of inputs converge on single cortical neurons, noisy discharges are difficult to achieve in most models of neural networks (Softky and Koch, 1993).

source: One exception is balanced networks, which have gained prominence in part because they produce irregular discharges as a result of chaotic dynamics (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012).

source: L4 neurons have variability close to the theoretical minimum. This implies that models of cortical networks should not explicitly aim to produce intrinsically noisy activity.

source: Other measurements in the barrel cortex have found highly variable responses to passive whisker deflection in L4 of anesthetized rats (Wang et al., 2010; Bale et al., 2013).

source: During anesthesia cortical activity is modulated by slow rhythms (e.g., up and down states), which are not observed during active behavior (Crochet and Petersen, 2006).

source: In addition, the movements underlying active sensation might recruit circuit mechanisms that reduce variability.

source: Neural coding of the timing of touch onset and whisking phase are key components of models of object localization (Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Kleinfeld and Deschenes, 2011).

source: In contrast, although many L4 cells are modulated by whisking phase, their low spike rates during whisker movements (mean <0.15 spikes/whisk cycle) hinders efficient decoding of whisking phase from population activity (Figure 4).

source: Mice were trimmed to a single C2 whisker to perform the discrimination.

claim: Whisker trajectories and shapes were automatically quantified using the Janelia Whisker Tracker.

evidence: The manuscript describes the method used for whisker tracking.

claim: Contact periods with the pole were automatically determined by pole proximity and whisker curvature using custom Matlab routines and manually curated to ensure 1 millisecond accuracy.
source: Contact periods with the pole were automatically determined by pole proximity and whisker curvature using custom Matlab routines (https://github.com/hireslab/HLab_Whiskers) and manually curated to ensure 1 millisecond accuracy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for determining touch times.

claim: On the day of the first recording, a small craniotomy (∼200 µm diameter) was made over the C2 barrel column determined by transcranial intrinsic signal imaging.
source: On the day of the first recording, a small craniotomy (∼200 µm diameter) was made over the C2 barrel column determined by transcranial intrinsic signal imaging (O'Connor et al., 2010).

source: Recordings targeting cortical L4 were obtained with patch pipettes pulled from borosilicate tubing (Sutter instrument, CA) and an Axopatch 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices).

source: Cells were recorded blindly (DeWeese et al., 2003).

source: Recordings in L4 with the midpoint of the DiI track <160 µm from the center of C2 were considered in C2 (31 recordings) and those >200 µm but still in the barrel field (10 recordings) were considered outside of C2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: L5 recordings ranged 98–324 µm from the center of C2 (near C2).
source: L5 recordings ranged 98–324 µm from the center of C2 (near C2).

source: Recordings with unstable spike rate across the behavioral session were excluded.

source: Recordings were repeated for 1–5 days per animal.

claim: The peak touch rate was the highest mean spikes per bin (1 ms) of the cell's PCTHs, typically corresponding to the first touch.
source: The peak touch rate (Figure 2) was the highest mean spikes per bin (1 ms) of the cell's PCTHs, typically corresponding to the first touch.
evidence: The manuscript defines how peak touch rate was calculated.

claim: Spike onset latency is the time between the touch onset and where the rise of the PCTH exceeds the pretouch mean (−50 to 0 ms pre-onset) by two standard deviations.
source: Spike onset latency is the time between the touch onset and where the rise of the PCTH exceeds the pretouch mean (−50 to 0 ms pre-onset) by two standard deviations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript defines how spike onset latency was calculated.

claim: Active exploration epochs are whisking epochs, including touch epochs (excluding prolonged touches, > 100 ms).
source: Active exploration epochs are whisking epochs, including touch epochs (excluding prolonged touches, > 100 ms).
evidence: The manuscript defines what constitutes active exploration epochs.

claim: Half of the data was used to find the optimal threshold and the other half of the data to predict the performance of the decoder.
source: We used half of the data to find the optimal threshold and the other half of the data to predict the performance of the decoder.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cross-validation procedure for decoder evaluation.

claim: A multinomial naïve Bayes classifier was trained to report for every time point what was the most likely time elapsed from touch onset.
source: We trained a multinomial naïve Bayes classifier (Duda et al., 2001) to report for every time point what was the most likely time elapsed from touch onset, with a root mean square time error derived from boostrapping (100 runs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for decoding time from touch and cites the classifier method.

claim: To decode whisking phase, it was assumed that the preferred phase was uniformly distributed.
source: To decode the whisking phase we assumed that the preferred phase was uniformly distributed.
evidence: The manuscript describes an assumption made in the whisking phase decoding analysis.

claim: Under the assumption of independent neural responses, simulations show several-fold more information about touch in C2 than non-C2 and poor performance in decoding whisking phase.
source: Under the assumption of independent neural responses, our simulations show several-fold more information about touch in C2 than non-C2 and poor performance in decoding whisking phase (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the decoding results with a caveat about the independence assumption.

claim: Other factors, such as correlated activity among neurons, can impact the accuracy of the population code and the exact information carried by touch and whisking phase, but this is unlikely to alter the qualitative picture presented here.
source: Other factors, such as correlated activity among neurons, can impact the accuracy of the population code (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014) and the exact information carried by touch and whisking phase, but this is unlikely to alter the qualitative picture presented here.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations of the decoding analysis while asserting the robustness of the main conclusions.

claim: To reduce adaptation effects, touch epochs were selected in which the inter contact interval (ICI) was longer than 250 ms.
source: To reduce adaptation effects we selected touch epochs in which the inter contact interval (ICI) was longer than 250 ms.
evidence: The manuscript describes a method for controlling for adaptation in the Fano factor analysis.

claim: The remaining touch events were divided into five groups (N, number of points per group; minimum, 20), clustered by touch characteristics.
source: We divided the remaining touch events into five groups (N, number of points per group; minimum, 20), clustered by touch characteristics.

source: We z-scored pretouch velocity and the maximum curvature change shortly after touch (0–20 ms).

source: For each neuron we clustered the touch events using a density-based clustering method (OPTICS; [Cunningham and Yu, 2014]).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering algorithm used and cites the method.

claim: The FF was calculated by counting spikes in sliding windows of 10 ms for each cell and each of the five bins.
source: We calculated the FF by counting spikes in sliding windows of 10 ms for each cell and each of the five bins (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for calculating Fano factors.

claim: Confidence intervals for the FFs were obtained by resampling 1000 times.
source: Confidence intervals for the FFs were obtained by resampling 1000 times.

claim: FFs were also computed using a Poisson process with absolute refractory period, with average touch response matched to the data.
source: We also computed FFs using a Poisson process with absolute refractory period, with average touch response matched to the data (Berry II and Meister, 1998) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: There were no significant changes in firing rate between whisking and non-whisking across the L4 population (L4 inside C2, p = 0.75; L4 outside C2, p = 0.92).
source: There were no significant changes in firing rate between whisking and non-whisking across the L4 population (L4 inside C2, p = 0.75; L4 outside C2, p = 0.92), whereas L5 showed a modest, but significant increase with whisking (p = 0.019, Wilcoxon signed rank).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing firing rates during different behavioral states.

claim: L5 showed a modest, but significant increase in firing rate with whisking (p = 0.019, Wilcoxon signed rank).
source: There were no significant changes in firing rate between whisking and non-whisking across the L4 population (L4 inside C2, p = 0.75; L4 outside C2, p = 0.92), whereas L5 showed a modest, but significant increase with whisking (p = 0.019, Wilcoxon signed rank).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results for L5 firing rate changes.

claim: Modulation by whisking phase was not significantly different between L4 neurons inside and outside the C2 barrel (p = 0.68).
source: Modulation by whisking phase was not significantly different between L4 neurons inside and outside the C2 barrel (p = 0.68), but both were significantly more phase modulated than L5 (p = 4.3e-5 and p = 0.012 respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing phase modulation across different neuron populations.

claim: Both L4 inside and outside C2 were significantly more phase modulated than L5 (p = 4.3e-5 and p = 0.012 respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum).
source: Modulation by whisking phase was not significantly different between L4 neurons inside and outside the C2 barrel (p = 0.68), but both were significantly more phase modulated than L5 (p = 4.3e-5 and p = 0.012 respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing phase modulation between L4 and L5.

claim: 4.6 ± 8.7% of spikes were purely phase coupled in L4 C2, vs 23.8 ± 27.9% outside of C2 and 7.6 ± 14.9% in L5.
source: Subtraction of the touch spikes from touch and phase spikes reveals that 4.6 ± 8.7% of spikes were purely phase coupled in L4 C2, vs 23.8 ± 27.9% outside of C2 and 7.6 ± 14.9% in L5.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of purely phase-coupled spikes across different regions.

claim: During object localization, the majority of spikes in L4 excitatory neurons encode aspects of touch of the primary whisker, with many of the remaining spikes encoding whisking phase.
source: We conclude that during object localization, the majority of spikes in L4 excitatory neurons encode aspects of touch of the primary whisker, with many of the remaining spikes encoding whisking phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spike coupling analysis.

claim: Touch times could be reliably and precisely decoded by pooling activity from a handful of L4 neurons.
source: Touch times could be reliably and precisely decoded by pooling activity from a handful of L4 neurons (Figure 4) (Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the decoding analysis, citing a relevant reference.

claim: A decoder reading L4 activity can determine which whisker makes contact with millisecond temporal precision.
source: This implies that a decoder reading L4 activity can determine which whisker makes contact with millisecond temporal precision (Panzeri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding results, citing a relevant reference.

claim: The timing of spikes in L4 barrel cortex provides only a coarse representation of whisking phase.
source: Thus, the timing of spikes in L4 barrel cortex provides only a coarse representation of whisking phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the poor decoding performance for whisking phase.

claim: The deep modulation index of sensory responses to tactile stimulus features indicates that stimulus variability likely accounts for a significant component of variability in the touch response.
source: The deep modulation index of sensory responses to tactile stimulus features indicates that stimulus variability likely accounts for a significant component of variability in the touch response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modulation index measurements.

claim: Based on observations of whisker behavior it is possible to predict brief time windows when a neuron will fire a single or small number of spikes, as well as time periods when the spike probability is zero.
source: Based on observations of whisker behavior it is possible to predict brief time windows when a neuron will fire a single or small number of spikes, as well as time periods when the spike probability is zero.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal coupling of spikes to behavior.

claim: Touch detection by neurons from surrounding barrels (>200 µm from the principal whisker) was poor.
source: Touch detection by neurons from surrounding barrels (>200 µm from the principal whisker) was poor (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the decoding analysis.

claim: The poor performance of the decoder for whisking phase is related to the low spike rate during whisker movements.
source: The poor performance of the decoder is related to the low spike rate during whisker movements.
evidence: This is an explanation for the poor decoding performance of whisking phase.

claim: For a Poisson process, FF = 1, independent of the window size.
source: For a Poisson process, FF = 1, independent of the window size.
evidence: This is a statement of established statistical knowledge about Poisson processes.

claim: For a mean spike count equal to 0.5/touch, the minimum FF is produced with one spike in half of the trials.
source: For example, for a mean spike count equal to 0.5/touch, the minimum FF is produced with one spike in half of the trials (DeWeese et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical minimum FF, citing a reference.

claim: For mean spike count <1 the minimum FF corresponds to binomial spiking, with FF = 1- mean spike count.
source: For mean spike count <1 the minimum FF corresponds to binomial spiking, with FF = 1- mean spike count (Berry et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical minimum FF for low spike counts, citing a reference.

claim: FF is ∼1 before touch occurs because the mean spike count is very low (∼0.03), which implies a minimum possible Fano factor of ∼1.
source: Fano factor is ∼1 before touch occurs because the mean spike count is very low (∼0.03), which implies a minimum possible Fano factor of ∼1.
evidence: This is an explanation for why FF is high before touch, based on the low spike rate.

claim: Around the peak of the touch response the mean spike count is high (∼0.7), allowing detection of spiking statistics that differ from the Poisson distribution.
source: In contrast, around the peak of the touch response the mean spike count is high (∼0.7), allowing us to detect spiking statistics that differ from the Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is an explanation for why deviations from Poisson statistics can be detected after touch.

claim: Comparing simulations with actual spike trains revealed that L4 neuron response precision could not be explained by the refractory period alone.
source: Comparing the simulations with actual spike trains revealed that L4 neuron response precision could not be explained by the refractory period alone (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing observed FFs to simulated Poisson processes with refractory periods.

claim: Response variability was very large (FF = 6.57 mean ± 5.41 s.d.) when ignoring the millisecond time scale of behavior.
source: Response variability was very large (FF = 6.57 mean ± 5.41 s.d.) when we ignored the millisecond time scale of behavior (Figures 6E and 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of FF under different analysis conditions.

claim: Integrating activity in time windows as wide as average touch response periods (38 ms) gave a FF of 1.59 ± 0.49 when randomly sampling from the trial.
source: Integrating activity in time windows as wide as average touch response periods (38 ms) gave a FF of 1.59 ± 0.49 (Berry II and Meister, 1998) (Figures 6E, 2) when randomly sampling from the trial, and FF of 1.37 ± 0.74 (Figures 6E, 3) when aligned to touch onset.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of FF under different analysis conditions.

claim: Integrating activity in time windows of 38 ms aligned to touch onset gave a FF of 1.37 ± 0.74.
source: Integrating activity in time windows as wide as average touch response periods (38 ms) gave a FF of 1.59 ± 0.49 (Berry II and Meister, 1998) (Figures 6E, 2) when randomly sampling from the trial, and FF of 1.37 ± 0.74 (Figures 6E, 3) when aligned to touch onset.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of FF under different analysis conditions.

claim: Excitatory neurons in L4 of barrel cortex exhibit almost noiseless responses to touch.
source: Together, these results show that excitatory neurons in L4 of barrel cortex exhibit almost noiseless responses to touch.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the Fano factor analysis.
